      "evidence_text": "User: Can you explain how a B-tree index makes lookups faster in a database? Assistant: A B-tree keeps keys sorted in wide, shallow nodes. Each node holds many keys and pointers to children, so a lookup starts at the root, compares the key with the few values in that node, and follows exactly one pointer down. Because every node is wide, even a table with millions of rows is usually only three or four levels deep, which means three or four page reads instead of scanning every row. Range queries are cheap too: once the first matching key is found, the leaves are linked, so the database walks along them in order. The cost is on writes. Every insert or update to an indexed column must also update the tree, and occasionally split a full node. That is why indexing every column is a bad idea: reads on the indexed columns get faster while every write gets slower, and the indexes take disk space. A good rule is to index the columns that appear in frequent WHERE clauses and joins, check the query plan to confirm the index is used, and drop indexes nothing reads."

      "evidence_text": "User: What do the Cache-Control and ETag headers actually do in HTTP? Assistant: They answer two different questions. Cache-Control tells a browser or proxy how long it may reuse a response without asking the server again: max-age is the number of seconds, no-store forbids keeping it at all, and private means only the user's own browser may keep it, not a shared proxy. An ETag is a label for one version of a resource, often a hash of its content. When the cached copy expires, the browser sends the label back in an If-None-Match header. If the content has not changed, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, which saves bandwidth even though a round trip still happens. Used together they give fast pages without stale data: long max-age for files whose names change when their content changes, such as bundled scripts with a hash in the file name, and short max-age plus an ETag for pages that change in place. The most common mistake is caching a personalised page in a shared proxy, which is exactly what private exists to prevent."
